explain.say: Why do we spell name with an a and bite with an i, when they do not sound like those letters anywhere else in Europe? Because your spelling is frozen speech from the 1400s. The timeline shows how English changed.

explain.say: Look at 1066. After the Norman Conquest, French became the language of the court, so we got pairs like cow and beef, pig and pork: English in the field, French on the plate. Old English word endings wore away, and Middle English, Chaucer's English, grew. Which French word have you used today?

explain.say: From about 1400, the long vowels moved up in the mouth, like people shuffling along a bench. Look at the chain: bite was beet-uh, house was hoos, meet sounded like mate, name was nah-muh. The top vowels had nowhere to go, so they split into two sounds. Say bite the old way!

explain.say: And the spelling? Caxton's printing press came in 1476, right in the middle of the shift. Printers fixed spellings while the sounds kept moving. That is why knight keeps a k and gh that Chaucer actually pronounced. Look at the word split up. Which silent letters can you think of?

explain.say: By Shakespeare's day much of the shift was done, and Johnson's Dictionary of 1755 settled spelling. The Danish linguist Otto Jespersen named the shift, and scholars still debate its cause. Well done. Challenge: find three words whose spelling still preserves an old pronunciation.

faq.q: What was the Great Vowel Shift?
faq.a: A change in English pronunciation, roughly 1400 to 1700, in which long vowels moved higher in the mouth and the highest ones became diphthongs, so bite, once said like beet, became bite.

faq.q: When did the Great Vowel Shift happen?
faq.a: Mostly between about 1400 and 1700, beginning after Chaucer and largely complete by the late 1600s, though dates vary for different vowels.

faq.q: Why does English spelling not match pronunciation?
faq.a: Printing, from 1476, helped fix spellings while the Great Vowel Shift was still changing the sounds. Spelling stayed put and speech moved on.

faq.q: How did the Norman Conquest change English?
faq.a: After 1066 French became the language of power, adding thousands of words, like beef and justice, while English lost most of its old word endings and became Middle English.

faq.q: Who named the Great Vowel Shift?
faq.a: The Danish linguist Otto Jespersen, in his work on English grammar early in the twentieth century.

facts: William Caxton set up England's first printing press at Westminster in 1476.
Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language was published in 1755.
Otto Jespersen coined the name Great Vowel Shift.
